Key supporting findings: acute severe erythema within hours of a beach (sun) exposure followed by persistent darkening; distribution limited to sun‑exposed sites (dorsal hands/forearms/feet, V‑neck, face) with sparing under sandal straps; temporal relationship with hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) started 4 months earlier and no other new topical/oral exposures reported; high‑quality photos documenting hyperpigmentation and absence of blisters, skin fragility, mucosal or palmar involvement (making porphyria cutanea tarda and systemic hyperpigmentation less likely); and absence of suggestive features of phytophotodermatitis (no linear/bizarre streaks or known plant/citrus contact) or polymorphous light eruption (which usually recurs with subsequent exposures and is pruritic/papular rather than diffuse postinflammatory pigmentation). HCTZ is a well‑recognized photosensitizer capable of producing phototoxic dermatitis that acutely erythematizes then hyperpigments sun‑exposed skin.

Red flags / critical tests not present but not necessary to make a working diagnosis in this context: explicit documentation of mucosal/palmar pigmentation (negative by history/photos), liver disease history or LFTs (would be relevant if porphyria suspected), repeat episodes on re‑exposure (would help differentiate PMLE), and formal porphyrin testing only if blistering/fragility or chronic course were present. Given the clear temporal and clinical pattern, these omissions do not substantially weaken the diagnosis.

[DECISION] PASS
